analysis.one_liner: Protects federal red rock canyon lands in Utah as permanent wilderness, closing them to mining and drilling.
analysis.headline: With 14 cosponsors including one Republican, the bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee on the day it was introduced, never received a committee vote, and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would add hundreds of named areas across nine regions of Utah — from the Great Basin deserts to the Book Cliffs — to the National Wilderness Preservation System, the highest level of federal land protection. Wilderness designation keeps the land open for hiking, hunting, and other quiet recreation, but permanently closes it to new mining claims, oil and gas leasing, and geothermal leasing. It also reserves federal water rights for the areas, compensates Utah with land swaps for any state school-trust parcels caught inside the boundaries, and allows existing livestock grazing to continue.
analysis.who_benefits: The general public — especially hikers, hunters, paddlers, and future generations — gains permanent protection of some of the country's most scenic canyon country, including habitat for bighorn sheep, elk, and the largest free-roaming buffalo herd in the United States. The bill's own findings point to popular recreation areas near Arches and Canyonlands national parks and along the Green River.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hikers, hunters, paddlers, and future generations

how_it_helps.text: Designates hundreds of specific areas across nine Utah regions as components of the National Wilderness Preservation System, including areas adjacent to national parks and popular river corridors.

Withdraws the designated federal land from entry, appropriation, location and patent under mining law, and from disposition under mineral and geothermal leasing laws, permanently barring new extraction on the land.
Reserves federal water rights for each wilderness area with a priority date of enactment, protecting stream flows within the protected canyons.
Protects the Cedar Mesa archaeological area, which the bill's findings describe as suffering vandalism and theft of cultural resources.

analysis.who_pays: Mining, oil and gas, and geothermal companies lose access to the designated federal lands for new claims and leases. Off-road vehicle users and motorized outfitters lose ground open to motorized travel. The state of Utah gives up school-trust parcels inside the boundaries, though the bill requires the Interior Secretary to exchange them for federal land of approximately equal value.
analysis.who_pays_short: Mining and energy companies seeking new leases

drawbacks.text: Wilderness designation permanently forecloses mineral and energy development on the designated lands, which supporters of development argue could produce jobs, royalty revenue, and domestic resource production in a state where much of the land is federally owned.

The bill is pushed by an Illinois senator and carries 14 cosponsors from other states, while the lands in question are entirely in Utah — a recurring criticism that outsiders are setting land-use policy for a state they do not represent.

The bill entrenches existing livestock grazing inside the new wilderness areas, allowing grazing authorized at enactment to continue indefinitely, a concession conservation critics have long noted limits the ecological benefit of designation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is permanent and wide-reaching for the public — recreation, scenery, wildlife, water, and archaeological sites — while the costs fall on industries seeking future extraction on the affected parcels and on motorized recreation users. The trade is a genuine one, but the bill's carve-outs for existing grazing and its land-exchange compensation for Utah moderate the burden. The main weakness is political rather than design: with no Utah support beyond one Republican cosponsor, it had no realistic path in a committee controlled by members who would face the political fallout in Utah.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee on May 12, 2011, the committee never took it up, and the bill died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Durbin introduced the bill on May 12, 2011 with original cosponsors including Sens. Lieberman, Whitehouse, Cardin, and Reed, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources that same day.
Fourteen senators cosponsored the bill: 11 Democrats, 1 Independent, and 1 Republican.
No further action appears in the record after the referral — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — and the Congress ended on January 3, 2013 without the bill advancing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mining, oil and gas, and geothermal interests retain access to the federal lands for potential claims and leases, and motorized recreation users keep the ground that would have been closed. No land will be added to the National Wilderness Preservation System under this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mining and energy interests keep the land open

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was nearly all Democratic — 11 Democrats and 1 Independent joined 1 Republican among its 14 cosponsors — and neither chamber ever reached a vote.

industries.industry: Mining and hardrock mineral claim holders
industries.note: The bill withdraws the designated federal land from location, entry, and patent under mining law, ending new claim staking there. Wilderness protection preserves the land for the public, so the industry's access runs against the public's interest in this bill.

Designated land is withdrawn from disposition under mineral and geothermal leasing laws, closing it to future leasing. Energy development of scenic canyon country is exactly what the designation prevents.

The bill allows grazing authorized at enactment to continue inside the new wilderness areas, subject to regulation. Existing permit holders keep their livelihood even as the land around them gets the strictest federal protection.

Wilderness rules bar motorized and mechanized travel, closing roads and trails within the boundaries to off-road vehicles and mountain bikes. The public gains quiet recreation while motorized users lose terrain.
Permanent protection of canyon country, park-adjacent lands, and wild rivers safeguards the scenery and wildlife that drive Utah's recreation economy.
